extracted.intended_audience: regulated entities (EGUs), pipeline operators, state and Federal permitting agencies, and public commenters on EPA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating CO2 pipeline and sequestration feasibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and supporting analysis used by EPA to determine whether CO2 transport (pipelines) and geologic sequestration are 'adequately demonstrated' and feasible as part of a regulatory Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) determination. Includes permitting, siting, safety, capacity, and timeline considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA compliance and level of review (EA vs EIS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal actions (e.g., funding a CCS project) must generally comply with NEPA, which often requires that an environmental assessment (EA) or environmental impact statement (EIS) be conducted to consider environmental impacts of the proposed action, including consideration of reasonable alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An EA determines whether or not a Federal action has the potential to cause significant environmental effects; agencies issue a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) if not. Some projects may be categorically excluded. EISs are prepared where actions significantly affect the quality of the human environment. Determination depends on whole-project potential for significant impacts (e.g., crossings of sensitive habitats, cultural resources, wetlands, public safety concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA statutory timeline expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiscal Responsibility Act amendments established deadlines for NEPA reviews: environmental assessments must be completed within 1 year and environmental impact statements must be completed within 2 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lead agency unable to meet the deadline may extend it in consultation with the applicant to only so much additional time as is necessary to complete the EA or EIS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting timelines vary by site characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting timelines for CO2 pipelines and sequestration sites may vary depending on site characteristics (e.g., pipeline length, whether a project crosses a water of the U.S., whether the route crosses Federal land) and funding source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pipelines through BLM, USFS, or other Federal land are subject to NEPA. EPA anticipates pipelines that need only an EA could take ~2.5 years to permit, with possibly an additional year if an EIS is required; timelines depend on specific circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights-of-way acquisition feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful acquisition of rights-of-way easements for thousands of miles of pipeline across multiple ownership regimes demonstrates feasibility of ROW acquisition for pipeline projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include rerouting to avoid opposition, acquiring ROW across state, private, and Federal lands (e.g., Cedar Creek Anticline pipeline). Demonstrated mitigation (e.g., for endangered species habitat) can enable ROW through sensitive areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAST-41 / Permitting Council participation optionality and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects that opt in to the FAST-41 process are eligible for a more transparent and predictable review process and are tracked on the Permitting Dashboard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAST-41 standardizes interagency consultation; participation is voluntary; USE IT Act clarified CCS projects and CO2 pipelines are eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of siting tools and route-planning databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Community engagement and siting tools (e.g., NETL's CCS Pipeline Route Planning Database) should be used to support pipeline routing decisions and increase transportation safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Database includes state-specific regulations, energy and social justice factors, land use requirements, existing infrastructure, and areas of potential risk; it produces weighted values 0–1 where 0 = acceptable placement and 1 = avoid. The siting tool aims to avoid areas that would pose permitting challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance-to-sequestration as proxy for pipeline complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance to the nearest sequestration site (EPA uses 100 km / 62 miles) is a useful proxy for considerations related to complexity of pipeline construction and permitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA modeled unique distances and found most capacity is within 100 km; for units >100 km away, interstate pipelines and crossing multiple state authorities increase complexity. The 100 km assumption is an economic modeling assumption based on NETL studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: RULOF provisions for extended compliance timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to the RULOF provisions of 40 CFR 60.2a(e)-(h), a state can demonstrate a fundamental difference between information relevant to a particular affected EGU and the information EPA considered for the subcategory, warranting a longer compliance schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere fact that a pipeline crosses state boundaries is not alone sufficient; a confluence of factors (including interstate crossing plus other hurdles) must make meeting the deadline unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER premise: point-to-point (shorter) pipelines vs national trunkline
rubrics_metrics.description: The BSER analysis is not premised on the buildout of a national, trunkline CO2 pipeline network; it assumes most EGUs will use shorter, point-to-point pipeline segments to nearby sequestration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter pipelines (e.g., <100 km) are expected to be less challenging to permit and build; examples cited (ADM Decatur, 1.18 miles; Air Products 12 miles) required only EAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: PHMSA regulatory framework for CO2 pipeline safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety of CO2 pipelines transporting supercritical CO2 is regulated by PHMSA, including standards related to pipeline design, construction and testing, operations and maintenance, operator reporting requirements, operator qualifications, corrosion control and pipeline integrity management, incident reporting and response, and public awareness and communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA has authority to inspect operations and issue notices for noncompliance; PHMSA has initiated further rulemaking post-Satartia and issued advisories and research solicitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: State delegation and adoption of federal safety standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain states have authority delegated from DOT to conduct safety inspections and enforce state and Federal pipeline safety regulations for intrastate CO2 pipelines; federal law requires certified state authorities to adopt safety standards at least as stringent as the Federal standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA's state partners employ ~70% of all pipeline inspectors; they cover >80% of regulated pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator operational controls and reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 pipeline operators must take steps such as use of pressure monitors to detect leaks or initiate shut-off valves, annual reporting on operations, structural integrity assessments, and inspections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These controls, together with PHMSA and state standards, are designed to ensure captured CO2 is securely conveyed to sequestration sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrated safety record and incident reporting considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing CO2 pipelines have operated for over 60 years; data on incidents (e.g., PHMSA reported 102 CO2 pipeline incidents 2003–2022 with one injury and zero fatalities) and notable failures (Satartia 2020) inform safety assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Satartia incident highlighted atypical atmospheric/topographical conditions, emergency responder notification failures, and prompted PHMSA investigations, advisories, enforcement actions, and rulemaking to strengthen oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of geologic sequestration (broad availability requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geologic sequestration (long-term containment of CO2 in subsurface formations) is broadly available in the U.S.; deep saline formations are the most widely available and well understood option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses by DOE and USGS show widespread potential; nearly every state has or is close to formations with sequestration potential, and the total storage potential greatly exceeds projected CO2 volumes under the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key geological requirement: low permeability seal
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a low permeability seal is an important component of demonstrating secure geologic sequestration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Site characterization and subsurface studies are used to determine suitability for regional-scale storage and to demonstrate trapping and containment processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple formation types acceptable for sequestration
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequestration formations may include deep saline formations, unmineable coal seams, and oil and gas reservoirs (including EOR/EGR), and other formations (e.g., basalt) may also be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EOR and enhanced gas recovery have long operational histories; unmineable coal seams and depleted reservoirs provide additional storage options and may include existing infrastructure that can be repurposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration evidence through projects and programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale field research, demonstration projects, and permitting experience (e.g., DOE Regional Carbon Sequestration Partnerships, CarbonSAFE, existing UIC Class VI permits and applications) are evidence that geologic sequestration is adequately demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Regional partnerships injected >12 million tons (no indicated negative health/environmental impacts); CarbonSAFE projects progressing through Phases I–III; multiple UIC Class VI permits issued or under review; international projects (Sleipner, Snohvit, Quest, CarbFix) and domestic EOR operations support feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of sequestration capacity relative to projected emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE and USGS volumetric estimates indicate sequestration potential (trillions of metric tons) far exceed estimated CO2 emissions reductions under the rule (estimated 1.3–1.4 billion metric tons over 2028–2047).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA compares estimated sequesterable volume to rule emissions and concludes storage capacity is more than adequate (rule emissions <0.1% of some estimates of saline formation capacity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inventories and spatial analyses for siting feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA performed a geographic availability analysis using DOE/NETL/USGS resources, existing/probable pipelines, and areas within 100 km of potential sequestration sites to assess feasibility for coal-fired EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results: majority of capacity within short distances (e.g., >50% <32 km; 80% <100 km); EPA uses these inventories to support conclusions about pipeline and sequestration feasibility.
